extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, playwrights, actors, and educated readers (early-18th-century literary/theatrical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing, judging, and applying wit in poetry, prose, and the theatre — including taste, characterisation, and social etiquette related to 'wit' and 'fine breeding'. Draws on examples from classical and contemporary writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as 'Propriety of Thoughts and Words'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If Wit has truly been defined as a Propriety of Thoughts and Words, then that definition will extend to all sorts of Poetry... Propriety of Thought is that Fancy which arises naturally from the Subject, or which the Poet adapts to it. Propriety of Words is the cloathing of these Thoughts with such Expressions as are naturally proper to them.' (Dryden quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: Wit should be appropriate to its subject in both idea and language. Guidance: avoid forced or ill-fitted expressions; ensure thoughts arise naturally from the subject and that word choice 'cloaths' those thoughts properly. Anti-pattern: witty phrases or conceits that do not suit the subject or feel tacked-on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as the foundation of thought (with cautious note on playful falsehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Truth is the first Quality, and, as it were, the foundation of Thought' (Bouhours). Yet another critic (Vavassor) argues 'Falsehood gives it often all its Grace, and is, as it were, the Soul of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: truth should underpin thought — truthful grounds make wit most sound. Guidance: favour authentic, truthful basis for wit; but recognise that in epigrams or certain playful forms, deliberate falsehood or fiction can heighten grace when used knowingly. Scoring note: prefer wit grounded in truth except where the genre conventionally rewards artful falsehood (epigrammatic flourish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and classical measure over 'Gothick' extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for 'the beautiful Simplicity of the old Greeks and Romans' and criticism of writers who, 'not being able to come up to the beautiful Simplicity... have endeavoured to supply its place with all the Extravagancies of an irregular Fancy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: aesthetic simplicity and classical restraint are marks of good taste. Guidance: avoid excessive ornament, irregular fancy, or baroque affectation that obscures sense. Example/anti-pattern: 'Gothick' affectations in poetry or architecture—ornament that substitutes for genuine form or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write for 'Les Petits Esprits' (mob readers) — avoid preferring quibble over sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Segrais's threefold distinction: lowest readers ('Les Petits Esprits') are 'who like nothing but the Husk and Rind of Wit, prefer a Quibble, a Conceit, an Epigram, before solid Sense and elegant Expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: authors should not pander to the lowest/common taste that values superficial or flashy conceits. Guidance: aim for 'solid Sense and elegant Expression' rather than mere quibble or epigram. Anti-pattern: tailoring work to elicit loud immediate applause at the expense of substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit can be produced by resemblance and by opposition (turns and antitheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Not only the Resemblance, but the Opposition of Ideas, does very often produce Wit... in several little Points, Turns and Antitheses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: techniques for producing wit include analogies/ressemblances and oppositions/antitheses. Guidance: employ turns, contrasts, and clever parallels thoughtfully; these are legitimate sources of wit when grounded in sense and truth. Note: these devices should not be mere exercises in ingenuity divorced from meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge theatrical writing by Reason, Truth, and Nature (not mere reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I shall always make Reason, Truth, and Nature the Measures of Praise and Dispraise; if those are for me, the Generality of Opinion is of no Consequence against me; if they are against me, the general Opinion cannot long support me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: evaluate plays and theatrical wit against standards of reason, truthfulness to human nature, and naturalness of representation. Guidance: popularity does not equal merit; inspect whether a play's celebrated features align with reason and nature. Example: assessing 'Sir Fopling Flutter' by whether characters embody honest and refined behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-consistency: 'a fine gentleman should be honest and refined'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I will take for granted, that a fine Gentleman should be honest in his Actions, and refined in his Language.' Critique of characters (e.g., Dorimant) who are knavish in design but styled as 'fine gentlemen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: character portrayals should accord with the labels and moral expectations attached to them. Guidance: avoid making heroes or celebrated figures act in ways that contradict their supposed virtues (e.g., a 'fine gentleman' depicted as a knave or clown). Anti-pattern: glamorising vice by assigning it to heroic roles without moral consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should not celebrate vice as merit — avoid building comedy on ruin of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that some celebrated comedies are 'a perfect Contradiction to good Manners, good Sense, and common Honesty... built upon the Ruin of Virtue and Innocence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: comedic depiction of immorality must not function as endorsement or as the sole basis of a work's merit. Guidance: satire and representation of vice are acceptable, but plays should not make corruption the play's standard of merit or invite admiration for vice without critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and wit must fit gender/role plausibly (avoid unnatural mixtures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection to characters (e.g., Mrs. Harriot) whose behaviour and speech are inconsistent with their supposed upbringing: 'it is unnatural that we are not made to understand how she that was bred under a silly pious old Mother... came to be so Polite.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: ensure plausibility of social background, voice, and manners — character development must explain how dispositions arise. Guidance: avoid jarring mixtures (a pious upbringing producing arch coquetry) unless the work provides psychological or situational justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and 'fine breeding': balance mind and body; gesture should follow thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of educating daughters only in person and sons only in mind; 'The true Art... To make the Mind and Body improve together; and if possible, to make Gesture follow Thought, and not let Thought be employed upon Gesture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: proper breeding/education trains both mind and body in tandem. Guidance for performers/writers: cultivate natural, meaning-driven gesture and deportment rather than mechanical 'steps' or ornamental affectations. Anti-pattern: training that produces hollow, performed grace divorced from inward sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation in social ritual (example: mourning fashion) — sincerity over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that mourning customs have become fashion and spectacle: 'This Fashion of Sorrow is now become a generous Part of the Ceremonial... Courtiers... are immediately seized with Grief from Head to Foot' and that ostentatious mourning distorts meaning and harms tradespeople.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: social rituals should retain their original sincere purpose rather than becoming mere fashionable display. Guidance: when evaluating social conduct (or its depiction), prefer authenticity and proportionate observance; beware of performative extremes that invert the ritual's meaning and produce economic or moral absurdities.
